system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old male with a history of kidney transplantation, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for in-stent restenosis of the right transplanted renal artery, presenting with elevated blood pressure. A transplant kidney ultrasound revealed significantly increased renal artery velocities, confirming restenosis. The patient underwent an elective angioplasty of the existing renal artery stent via endovascular approach using CO2 contrast, with no complications. He remained hemodynamically stable throughout, with preserved renal function post-procedure. Pain was controlled, and he tolerated advancement of diet and activity. He was discharged home on dual antiplatelet therapy, antihypertensives, immunosuppressants, and insulin, with instructions for wound care, activity restrictions, and follow-up with vascular surgery and transplant nephrology.
problems: Other complications due to genitourinary device, implant, and graft
Kidney replaced by transplant
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Unspecified essential hypertension
Pure hypercholesterolemia
Atherosclerosis of renal artery
Hyperplasia of prostate, unspecified, without urinary obstruction and other lower urinary symptoms (LUTS)
Surgical operation with implant of artificial internal device causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication,without mention of misadventure at time of operation
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of other urinary organs
Long-term (current) use of insulin

It is normal to have slight swelling of the legs:
Elevate your leg above the level of your heart (use ___

It is normal to feel tired and have a decreased appetite, your

It is important to eat nutritious food options (high fiber,

maintain your strength and assist in wound healing

softener while taking pain medication

You may shower (let the soapy water run over groin incision, 
rinse and pat dry)

amounts of drainage from the wound, then place a dry dressing or 
band aid over the area that is draining, as needed
No heavy lifting, pushing or pulling (greater than 5 lbs) for 
1 week (to allow groin puncture to heal)
After 1 week, you may resume sexual activity
After 1 week, gradually increase your activities and distance 
walked as you can tolerate
No driving until you are no longer taking pain medications
Call and schedule an appointment to be seen in ___ weeks for 
post procedure check and ultrasound

Numbness, coldness or pain in lower extremities 
Temperature greater than 101.5F for 24 hours
New or increased drainage from incision or white, yellow or 
green drainage from incisions
Bleeding from groin puncture site

pressure to area for 10 minutes. If bleeding stops, call 
vascular office ___. If bleeding does not stop, call 
___ for transfer to closest Emergency Room.

___

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Thompson. I’m Dr. Lee, one of the vascular surgery team. You’ve been admitted today because we found a narrowing in the artery that supplies blood to your transplanted kidney. We’re planning to do a procedure to open it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, doctor. I’ve had this before, right? Last year they put in a stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. The stent is still there, but it’s developed a narrowing inside — what we call in-stent restenosis. That’s why your blood pressure has been going up lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ah, that makes sense. My nurse at home said my pressures were high. So what are we going to do now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll do a balloon angioplasty. We go through a small puncture in your groin, thread a catheter up to the kidney artery, and use a balloon to reopen the narrowed area.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be asleep? I remember last time I was groggy afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll be under light sedation — not fully asleep, but relaxed and comfortable. The procedure is minimally invasive and usually goes very smoothly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And is it safe with my transplant and diabetes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve taken all that into account. You’ve been pre-hydrated to protect your kidney, and we’ve coordinated with transplant nephrology. Your labs look good, and your blood sugar is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been checking it like they told me. What about the medications I’m on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual meds — especially your immunosuppressants like tacrolimus and mycophenolate. We’ll also keep your insulin and blood pressure pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And after the procedure? Will I feel better right away?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Many patients notice their blood pressure improves quickly. But the main goal is to protect your kidney function over time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. How long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most people stay one to two days. We’ll watch you closely after the procedure, and if all goes well, you could go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, that sounds manageable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mr. Thompson, we’re about to head down to the endovascular suite. Any last questions before we start?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, doctor. I trust you. Just let me know when it’s done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Will do. You’ll wake up in the recovery area, and I’ll come talk to you afterward.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi again. You’re in the recovery unit. The procedure went perfectly. We opened up the narrowed part of the artery with the balloon. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. Is the stent still okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The stent is intact. The narrowing was inside it, so we dilated it with the balloon. We didn’t need to place a new stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my kidney? Is it getting good blood flow now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the angiogram showed much better flow after the angioplasty. That should help your kidney function and keep your blood pressure more stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. My brother had a heart stent — he’s on two blood thinners. Will I need that too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, actually. You’ll be on aspirin and Plavix — that’s clopidogrel — for at least a few months to prevent clots from forming in the stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I can do that. Any side effects I should watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Mainly bleeding — like if you notice bruising, nosebleeds, or blood in your stool. But it’s uncommon. We’ll keep the dose low to minimize risk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about the groin spot where they went in?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should heal quickly. Keep it clean and dry. You can shower tomorrow. Avoid heavy lifting for about a week to let it seal properly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No lifting — like how much?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nothing over five pounds — so no grocery bags, tools, or grandkids for a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Ha, I’ll tell my wife. What about driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off until you’re off pain meds. Probably a few days. Just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. Vital signs are stable, and your labs show your kidney function is unchanged — which is good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, if you’re feeling up to it. We’ll get your discharge papers ready. You’ll need to follow up with vascular surgery in two weeks for an ultrasound.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my transplant doctor too?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. Keep all your regular appointments. They’ll monitor your kidney and adjust meds as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, doctor. Thank you — I feel much better knowing we caught this early.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. You did great. Just take it easy for a few days, watch the incision, and call us if anything seems off — like swelling, fever, or bleeding.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Thompson. Get some rest at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I plan to — maybe even put my feet up like you said.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. That’s exactly what I like to hear.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 60-year-old male with a history of kidney transplantation, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for symptomatic in-stent restenosis of the right transplanted renal artery, presenting with elevated blood pressure. Ultrasound confirmed increased renal artery velocities. The patient underwent elective balloon angioplasty of the stenotic segment via right femoral access, with successful restoration of blood flow and no procedural complications. He remained hemodynamically stable throughout, with preserved renal function post-procedure. Pain was controlled, and he tolerated diet and ambulation well. He was discharged home on dual antiplatelet therapy, antihypertensives, immunosuppressants, and insulin, with instructions for wound care, activity restrictions, and follow-up with vascular surgery and transplant nephrology.
